  - Sputum culture conversion at 8 weeks does not map one-to-one to infectiousness reduction.
  - Fewer secondary cases are averted if the incidence trend and treated-share assumptions are already near saturation.
suggested_evidence: The literature on rapid infectiousness decline after starting effective therapy and on pre-diagnosis transmission supports the logic. I cannot name specific studies with confidence. UNGROUNDED, and the Verifier should find the most relevant modelling studies.
All numerical inputs are my own inference.

evidence_found: The guinea-pig data show infectiousness drops sharply with effective therapy regardless of culture status, which weakens the case that a faster culture conversion adds much extra transmission reduction.
In one MDR-TB guinea-pig experiment, patients infected 26.7% of animals before treatment and 27.8% at 72 hours after drug initiation.
Early post-start infectiousness is therefore not always near zero, which keeps some upper tail alive.
The ROSETTA trial found no substantive benefit of rosuvastatin on culture conversion.
If the trial under evaluation has a similarly weak conversion signal, this channel shrinks further. I can't confirm this for the actual trial.
caveats: "Infectiousness falls quickly after effective therapy starts": **VERIFIED.**
In early guinea-pig experiments, animals exposed to patients on effective treatment were only 2% as likely to be infected as those exposed to untreated patients.
A systematic review says data from diverse experimental studies suggest infectiousness declines rapidly after effective treatment starts, before smear and culture conversion.
A 2025 review says the exact duration remains uncertain.
"Most transmission occurs before diagnosis": **PLAUSIBLE, partly supported.**
A Valencia whole-genome-sequencing study found 5 of 14 cases (35.7%) likely transmitted well before symptom onset.
In rural China (Songjiang), 40.6% of determinate transmission events occurred before the index case's symptom onset.
These figures are for before symptom onset, not before diagnosis. Diagnostic delay would push the pre-diagnosis share higher.
A modelling study estimated roughly 68% of global transmission came from asymptomatic TB.
The range is wide (27–92%).

Post-start share of lifetime transmission is 1–5%: **UNVERIFIABLE, plausible.** The guinea-pig 2% figure and the pre-diagnosis shares are consistent with a small number. I found no direct estimate of this parameter.
"Culture conversion at 8 weeks does not map to infectiousness one-to-one": **VERIFIED.**

A WHO-commissioned meta-analysis found most patients remained culture positive at 2 weeks. It notes culture positivity is only one component of infectiousness, with cough frequency and aerosol generation also important.
It also states there are no data describing how infectiousness changed over time after treatment initiation.
This supports the Investigator's downward adjustment, and also means the 10–20% fractional reduction is poorly anchored.
Arithmetic: **VERIFIED.** 3.3M × 0.5 × 0.003 × 10 ≈ 50k, and ~20k after weighting.
10 DALYs per secondary case: **PLAUSIBLE.** It is consistent with Menzies' 12.1 DALYs per incident case.
revised_hypothesis:
- Most transmission occurs before treatment starts, and effective therapy rapidly reduces infectiousness. Culture conversion is an imperfect proxy for infectiousness, so the incremental transmission benefit is small.
- The specific figures (0.3% net reduction, 1–5% post-start share, 10–20% fractional reduction) are UNGROUNDED.
- Treat ~10–30k as an order-of-magnitude placeholder. The true value is probably at or below the low end if the trial's culture-conversion effect is weak.
- Strength: low. This is the least material of the three channels.
core_claim: The net reduction in total transmission from faster conversion is ~0.3% (range 0.1–1%).
core_claim_reason: Qualitative literature supports "small", but the 1–5% post-start share and the 10–20% fractional reduction are unsupported, and the evidence cuts toward a smaller effect.

original.thread_name: Unvalued benefits — post-TB lung disease, long-term post-treatment
original.title: The "lung benefit without mortality benefit" scenario is structurally less valuable than a simple p_success weighting implies
original.hypothesis:
The thread's framing suggests the unvalued channels might make the estimate "robust even if the on-treatment mortality effect is small." That holds only if a surrogate-only result still leads to adoption at similar scale. The Phase III endpoint, and what WHO guideline bodies require, determines this.
- If the trial's primary endpoint is something like unfavorable outcome or relapse rather than lung function, a lung-only benefit would not obviously earn a recommendation.
- Adoption would also require willingness to pay for an additional drug for 3.3M patients.
- This gives an adoption probability in the "mortality fails, lung holds" branch well below the 60% uptake CG assumes. I'd guess ≤10–20%, but this is UNGROUNDED.
original.mechanism:
This is a correction to how Critiques 1–3 are weighted, not a separate value term.
- Simple weighting: p_success × full uptake. If I naively applied the same 60% uptake in the lung-only branch, the lung channel would be up to ~2× higher (a probability of roughly 0.4 + 0.6 × P(lung holds | mortality fails) instead of 0.45).
- Realistic weighting, with P(lung holds | mortality fails) at 0.3–0.5 and conditional adoption of 10–20%, adds only ~0.02–0.06 to the 0.4 base. That supports the ~0.45 figure I used.
- Net effect: the lung channel is closer to 1× than 2× its p_success-weighted value, which limits the upside. Anyone who weights it by a "surrogate holds" probability alone without discounting for adoption will overstate it.
suggested_evidence: Logical and structural argument about regulatory and guideline pathways. I cannot identify a specific source for this trial's registered endpoints. UNGROUNDED.
The Verifier should check the Phase IIc and planned Phase III endpoints, and how WHO guideline development weighs lung-function surrogates.

evidence_found: Few tuberculosis treatment trials have included lung function as a primary efficacy outcome , although
FEV1 correlates with long-term mortality . This supports the premise that lung function is a non-standard endpoint, so a lung-only win may not translate cleanly into guidelines.
The phase 2 trial by Wallis et al. found that
CC-11050 and everolimus might enhance the recovery of FEV1 . FEV1 was therefore used as a preliminary efficacy signal, not as an established registrational endpoint.
Phase IIc in TB normally means the STEP design.

CRUSH-TB, for example, uses time to sputum culture negativity as its primary intermediate endpoint . A trial in this style would not natively produce a lung-function primary endpoint. This is circumstantial, because I could not identify the CG-funded trial.
caveats: "A surrogate-only (lung) result would not obviously lead to adoption at 60% scale."* **PLAUSIBLE, no direct evidence.** I found no WHO guideline text on how lung-function surrogates are weighed. I did not find the CG model, the specific trial, or its registered Phase IIc and Phase III endpoints, so these remain **UNVERIFIABLE**.
Conditional adoption of 10–20% in the "mortality fails, lung holds" branch.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** The Investigator already labels it UNGROUNDED.
The 0.45, 0.4 base and 60% uptake figures, and the 3.3M patients.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** These come from the CG model, which I could not access.
Arithmetic.*
The "realistic" range checks out: 0.6 × (0.3–0.5) × (0.1–0.2) ≈ 0.018–0.06.
The "naive" bound is overstated. 0.4 + 0.6 × (0.3–0.5) gives about 0.58–0.70, which is roughly 1.3–1.6× of 0.45, not "up to ~2×". A 2× result would need P(lung holds | mortality fails) near 1.

Direction label.* The critique argues that the 0.45 figure is about right and that the upside is limited. It is labelled "increases", which does not match that argument. Its net effect is closer to neutral. It is a caution against over-crediting the lung channel.
revised_hypothesis:
- Retain this as a **weighting caution, flagged UNGROUNDED**. Do not apply the full uptake to the lung-only branch without a separate adoption discount.
- The effect is modest: roughly +0.02–0.06 on a 0.4 base.
- Fix the "up to 2×" figure to about 1.3–1.6×. Treat the direction as neutral to slightly decreasing, with small magnitude.

---
core_claim: conditional adoption in the lung-only branch is far below 60% (about 10–20%).
core_claim_reason: the reasoning is plausible, and lung function is a non-standard TB endpoint, but I found no direct evidence on WHO or adoption behaviour for this branch.

original.thread_name: Unvalued benefits — post-TB lung disease, long-term post-treatment
original.title: The sweat-based diagnostic carries real option value but is speculative (~10–30k central)
original.hypothesis: CG assigns zero value to the sweat-based TB diagnostic funded alongside the trial. A non-sputum, point-of-care test could reach people who cannot produce sputum (children, people with HIV, those without access to labs). Roughly 2–3M TB cases per year are undiagnosed or unreported. A successful test could therefore add value on a scale comparable to the main intervention, but the probability of success is low and counterfactual diagnostics (tongue swabs and others) are advancing.
original.mechanism:
- P(reaches adoption): ~5%. This is UNGROUNDED; it is a typical early-stage-diagnostic base rate, not a figure from a source.
- Incremental cases detected beyond what alternative tests would detect (e.g., tongue-swab PCR): ~1–3% of incidence of ~10M, so ~100–300k cases per year.
- DALYs averted per additional case treated: ~5, assuming ~20% case fatality untreated × ~25 DALYs.
- Calculation: 0.05 × 200k × 5 ≈ 50k DALYs per year. Allowing for a delay before adoption and for counterfactual displacement, I discount this to ~10–30k. The range is 0 to ~100k.
- One consistency point for the Verifier: if the $7M all-in cost already includes the diagnostic's funding while the benefit is zero, the omission biases against the intervention. If it excludes the diagnostic funding, treating it as separate is defensible.
suggested_evidence: I cannot cite a specific source for the sweat-based test's development stage, accuracy, or regulatory path. UNGROUNDED.
The existence of competing non-sputum diagnostics (tongue swab, urine LAM) is an inference from the broader field. I have not checked current WHO endorsements.

evidence_found: WHO's tongue-swab recommendation has a limited scope.

Programmes may use tongue swabs from adults and adolescents when sputum cannot be obtained . Children and others who cannot give sputum are therefore not covered by that recommendation. This leaves some room for a different non-sputum test, which mildly supports the critique's option-value logic.

Against that, tongue swabs are less sensitive than sputum . The counterfactual is also moving fast. The base case for "incremental cases beyond alternatives" at 1–3% of incidence is therefore uncertain. Counterfactual displacement could push the value toward the low end.
The tongue-swab and NPOC tests are PCR-based. A sweat-based test would need its own evidence pathway and WHO policy review, which supports the low adoption probability.
caveats: CG funds a sweat-based TB diagnostic alongside the trial.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** I found nothing on this test's development stage, accuracy or regulatory path, or on the funding link.
Roughly 2–3M TB cases per year are undiagnosed or unreported.* **VERIFIED.**
8.3 million people were newly diagnosed with TB in 2024, which is 78% of the estimated incident cases .
Estimated incidence was 10.7 million , so the gap is about 2.4M.
Non-sputum competitors are advancing (tongue swab).* **VERIFIED, and ahead of the Investigator's expectation.**

WHO has issued its first recommendations on near-point-of-care molecular tests and easy-to-collect tongue swab samples , in February 2026. The Investigator had not checked WHO endorsements. The accuracy evidence is tongue-swab performance meeting the minimum WHO non-sputum target (>75% sensitivity, >98% specificity) .
Urine LAM as a competitor.* **PLAUSIBLE.** The LF-LAM assays are named in the WHO report as a bacteriological confirmation method.

Arithmetic.* 0.05 × 200k × 5 = 50k DALYs per year, which is correct. The 20% untreated case fatality and 25 DALYs per death are unverified assumptions. Widely cited untreated-TB fatality figures are higher than 20%, so these are not clearly inflated.
Whether the $7M all-in cost includes the diagnostic.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** I could not see the model. The Investigator correctly flags this as a consistency check for the CG model owner.
revised_hypothesis:
- CG assigns zero value to the sweat test. This may understate value, but the amount is speculative, and the range of 0 to ~100k DALYs per year is wide.
- The tongue-swab and NPOC WHO endorsement (Feb 2026) lowers the counterfactual incremental value relative to what the Investigator assumed. The paediatric and no-sputum gap remains.
- Mark it **UNGROUNDED, small magnitude, direction uncertain**.
- The cost-attribution question should be resolved from the model, not from this critique.

---
core_claim: P(adoption) ≈ 5% with an incremental yield of 1–3% of incidence, giving about 10–30k DALYs per year.
core_claim_reason: the arithmetic is internally consistent, but the probability and yield inputs are an assumed base rate with no source, and the test itself could not be found.

original.thread_name: Implementation — trial execution, guideline adoption pathway,
original.title: 60% steady-state uptake has no precedent among comparable TB program additions
original.hypothesis: CG's 60% is justified as "generic and cheap." Cost is only one of several determinants of uptake in TB programs. Comparable additions have often taken many years to reach even moderate coverage, and some stall below 50%. These include Xpert MTB/RIF (WHO endorsement 2010), the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen (WHO 2022), and adjunctive dexamethasone for TB meningitis (evidence 2004, widely recommended afterward). Adjunctive pyridoxine with isoniazid has also been recommended for years but is inconsistently supplied. An adjunct with no direct patient-visible benefit (it does not shorten treatment) and a separate pill is, if anything, a harder sell than diagnostics or regimens that simplify care. 60% is therefore plausibly an upper-bound or optimistic-case value, not a central one.
original.mechanism: adult_uptake enters roughly linearly. Reducing the long-run ceiling to 0.30–0.40 (the materiality line is 0.39) cuts SROI by 33–50%. Ramp shape matters little for a one-year speedup over an infinite horizon, because shifting any ramp by one year gains about (ceiling × one year of cases). So the ceiling matters much more than the ramp. The ramp only matters through a finite horizon, incidence decline and discounting (Thread 3).
suggested_evidence: Logical argument plus my recollection of precedents. I believe WHO Global TB Reports show that well over a decade after endorsement, Xpert/WRD was still the initial test for well under 100% of notified cases (roughly 40–50% in recent reports), but I cannot give an exact figure or citation, so this is UNGROUNDED as to numbers. I believe the dexamethasone-for-TBM and pyridoxine examples are real, but I cannot cite specific coverage data. Type of evidence: inference from precedents, not a direct study. The Verifier should pull WHO Global TB Report WRD-testing percentages by year and the HPMZ rollout data (GDF orders, number of countries adopting).

evidence_found: The analogs have key differences from a cheap generic oral adjunct. Xpert needs capital equipment and labs. HPMZ is supply-limited by rifapentine, and the NYC experience showed tolerability problems: only 14% of eligible patients were prescribed it, and 64% of those who started discontinued . Neither is a clean analog for generic-drug supply, so they bear on the ramp more than on the ceiling.
The global target is 100% WRD coverage by 2027 ( set at the 2023 UN high-level meeting
). A system target is not the same as steady-state achieved coverage, but it suggests over 50% is feasible with sustained push.
Equating adult_uptake with a coverage fraction among all patients may be a different construct from "percent of notified cases tested". I could not check how the CG model defines it.
caveats: Reducing the ceiling to 0.30–0.40 cuts SROI by 33–50%.* **VERIFIED as arithmetic.** 0.40/0.60 is a 33% cut and 0.30/0.60 is a 50% cut, assuming linear dependence. The model structure and the "0.39 materiality line" are unverifiable.
Comparable additions "often" stall below 50%.* **PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED.** Global WRD coverage is 54% after about 14 years and still rising, not stalled below 50%. WHO also reports that
37 of 49 high-burden countries used a WRD as the initial test for more than half of notified cases in 2024, up from 31 in 2023 . This is evidence of a slow ramp, not a ceiling.
An adjunct with no visible patient benefit is a harder sell.* **PLAUSIBLE, no direct evidence.** It is a reasonable argument.
The ramp matters little over an infinite horizon.* **LOGICALLY VALID**, with the discounting caveat the Investigator notes.
revised_hypothesis:
- Evidence supports the view that new TB tools take about 10 or more years to reach about 50% coverage, and that guideline endorsement does not guarantee uptake.
- This is a stronger argument against the ramp (timing) than against the ceiling. Its main effect is through discounting and finite horizons.
- Retain the ceiling concern as **UNGROUNDED**. Downgrade the magnitude from **large to medium**, with direction **decreases**.
- Do not use "stall below 50%" as support for the 0.30–0.40 ceiling. The WRD data point to 54% and rising.
- Dexamethasone and pyridoxine remain unverified. The pull the Investigator requested has been done for WRD and HPMZ. The GDF order data were not found.
core_claim: the long-run uptake ceiling is plausibly 0.30–0.40, not 0.60.
core_claim_reason: the precedents show slow ramps (HPMZ about 0.05% after three years, WRD 54% after about 14 years). None shows a stalled ceiling below 60% for a cheap, generic, oral co-administered drug.

original.thread_name: Implementation — trial execution, guideline adoption pathway,
original.title: A Phase III cannot be powered on mortality, so the WHO GDG would be recommending on surrogate or composite endpoints
original.hypothesis: CG's value is entirely mortality-based. If the modeled relative reduction (~10%) refers to mortality in DS-TB, a Phase III cannot feasibly detect it. On-treatment mortality in DS-TB is perhaps 3–6% in many settings, though higher with HIV or in severe disease. Detecting a 10% relative reduction from a 5% baseline (absolute 0.5 pp; alpha 0.05, power 80%) needs roughly 2 × (2.8)² × 0.0475 / 0.005² ≈ 30,000 per arm. That is my own calculation and rests on the assumed baseline. The realistic Phase III will therefore use relapse-free cure, unfavorable outcome, culture conversion or lung function. The GDG (GRADE) would then rate certainty down for indirectness on the mortality benefit. A recommendation could be delayed, made conditional, or made only for subgroups (e.g., high-risk, HIV-negative, severe disease). The adoption probability and uptake given a "positive" trial are therefore lower than CG's "if it works → 60%."
original.mechanism: This lowers adult_uptake (conditional recommendations produce lower uptake). It may also lengthen years_to_adoption if the GDG requests additional evidence. It also means the mortality effect that drives all benefits is never directly verified, which raises the variance of the realized relative_reduction (Thread 1). The direction is downward on uptake. Quantification is uncertain: a conditional recommendation limited to a subgroup (e.g., a third of patients) would cut effective uptake by about half or more, but that scenario is speculative.
suggested_evidence: Logical and statistical argument (sample size calculation above, which depends on the 5% and 10% inputs). On GRADE, I believe indirectness from surrogate outcomes is a standard downgrading criterion in the WHO handbook for guideline development, but the Verifier should check the handbook text. The baseline mortality figure is UNGROUNDED and needs a source (WHO Global TB Report treatment-outcome data).

evidence_found: Weakens the critique.** WHO TB guideline groups routinely treat composite patient-important outcomes (treatment success, unfavourable outcome including death, relapse) as critical outcomes.
The critique treats a composite as a weak substitute. In TB, a composite that includes death is often a direct outcome. That reduces the expected indirectness penalty.
This is from my background knowledge. I did not search for it.
Supports the critique.** The only statin RCT I found, StAT-TB, is a Phase 2b dose-finding trial.
Its endpoints are time to sputum-culture negativity and lung function.
Mortality is assessed as a tolerability measure.
Mortality is not the primary efficacy endpoint.
Observational data link statin use to lower all-cause mortality in TB patients with ASCVD.
The authors say RCTs are needed.
That is a narrow subgroup, and it supports the case for a subgroup-limited recommendation.
caveats: Sample size of about 30,000 per arm (5% baseline, 10% relative reduction, α 0.05, 80% power): VERIFIED (arithmetic).**
I recomputed it with the standard two-proportion formula: 7.84 × (0.0475 + 0.0430) / 0.005² ≈ 28,400 per arm. The Investigator's shortcut gives about 29,800. Both round to roughly 28–30k per arm.
The result depends entirely on the 5% baseline and the 10% effect, as the Investigator said.
On-treatment DS-TB mortality of about 3–6% (previously UNGROUNDED): PLAUSIBLE, now sourced.**
A program-setting cohort of drug-susceptible pulmonary TB found 37 of 565 patients (6.6%) died during the study period.
In Kenya, about 6% of drug-susceptible TB cases died.
A multi-country study reported mortality of 6.0% in adequately treated patients with pan-susceptible strains.
WHO reports DS-TB treatment success of 88% (2023 data).
That is consistent with deaths of roughly 4–6%, but I did not retrieve the exact WHO death proportion.
The "3–6%" range is therefore reasonable. Cohorts with HIV or severe disease run higher, so the range sits at the low-to-mid end of what is reported.
GRADE downgrades for indirectness when surrogate outcomes are used: VERIFIED.**
WHO SAGE guidance says that when important outcomes are represented by a surrogate, the evidence quality frequently needs down-rating for indirectness.
A WHO guideline applying the Handbook (2nd edition) downgrades for indirectness when the evidence differs from the target context in populations, interventions, comparisons or outcomes.
I did not retrieve the Handbook text itself. The two sources above are WHO documents applying it.
Recommendation delayed, conditional or subgroup-only: PLAUSIBLE.** This is a reasonable inference. It is not a documented outcome for any specific TB adjunct.
Effective uptake would fall by about half or more under a subgroup recommendation: UNVERIFIABLE.** The Investigator already flagged this as speculative.
revised_hypothesis:
A mortality-powered Phase III would need about 28–30k patients per arm at a 5–6% baseline. A mortality-driven benefit would therefore probably be inferred from composite or surrogate endpoints. That invites an indirectness downgrade. It could make the recommendation conditional, delayed or subgroup-limited, and it raises variance on the realized relative reduction. Counterweight: TB GDGs usually accept unfavourable-outcome composites that include death as direct. The uptake and timing effects are UNGROUNDED. **Magnitude: low-to-medium** (downgraded from medium). Direction: decreases.

---
core_claim: A Phase III cannot be powered on a roughly 10% relative mortality reduction (about 30k per arm), so the recommendation would rest on surrogate or composite endpoints that GRADE treats as indirect.
core_claim_reason: The arithmetic reproduces, baseline mortality sits in the claimed range, and WHO guidance confirms the downgrading mechanism. No evidence ties this to a specific uptake reduction.

original.thread_name: Implementation — trial execution, guideline adoption pathway,
original.title: Clinical eligibility and monitoring barriers cap the achievable prescribing share below the "generic and cheap" logic
original.hypothesis: TB treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide) is itself hepatotoxic, and anti-TB drug-induced liver injury occurs in a non-trivial minority of patients (commonly cited in the low single digits to ~10%, depending on setting and definition). Statins carry label warnings for active liver disease and transaminase elevation, and are historically avoided in pregnancy. Clinicians managing a TB patient with rising ALT will plausibly not want an additional agent that confounds attribution of DILI, and may stop it. Programs would likely require baseline and follow-up LFTs, which many NTP settings do not routinely perform for DS-TB. Also relevant are drug–drug interactions (rifampicin induction of CYP3A4; some protease-inhibitor-based ART raises atorvastatin exposure, while efavirenz lowers it) and pill-burden aversion. FDC regimens are valued precisely because they avoid extra pills.
original.mechanism: This reduces adult_uptake through (a) a smaller eligible population, (b) program reluctance, and (c) discontinuation. Inference-based illustrative arithmetic: excluding ~10–20% of adults for liver disease, DILI, pregnancy or women of reproductive age, polypharmacy and age, then applying a program-adoption factor, could move 0.60 to roughly 0.45–0.50 before adherence. This is my own illustrative scenario, not a sourced estimate. If LFT monitoring is mandated and not available, uptake could fall further, or monitoring costs (not in CG's cost) would be added.
suggested_evidence: Mixed. Statin labeling and CYP3A4 pharmacology are well-established. The Liverpool HIV/TB drug interaction resource is the right place to check specific ART interactions. Anti-TB DILI incidence ranges are in the literature but I cannot cite a specific paper. The specific exclusion shares are UNGROUNDED.

evidence_found: Statin identity matters.** The Phase 2b trial (StAT-TB) tests pravastatin.
It asks whether pravastatin adjunctive therapy shortens time to sputum-culture negativity and improves lung function.
In preclinical work, atorvastatin and mevastatin did not inhibit Mtb growth in THP-1 cells at nontoxic doses.
Pravastatin showed the least toxicity in that study.

From background knowledge, pravastatin is not substantially CYP3A4-metabolised. If CG's candidate is pravastatin, the CYP3A4 and PI-boosted ART interaction arguments largely fall away. The hepatotoxicity-attribution and pill-burden arguments remain.
I do not know which statin CG assumes. The Investigator should have flagged that dependence.
The DILI meta-analysis authors say regular liver function monitoring is imperative during anti-TB treatment.
This supports the premise that monitoring is a live issue, though it is not specific to statins.
caveats: Anti-TB DILI is common, "low single digits to ~10%": PARTIALLY VERIFIED.**
A recent meta-analysis reported a global incidence of 11.5%, with rates varying from 2% to 28%.
Another source cites 3–36% for drug-susceptible TB.
Incidence varies with the cohort, regimen, DILI threshold and monitoring.

The Investigator's range is directionally right but understates the upper end. If anything, DILI is more common than stated, which strengthens the premise. The Investigator said they could not cite a paper. Wang et al. (2022), a meta-analysis of 160 studies, is the relevant one.
Rifampicin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer: VERIFIED.**
Rifampin is a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and 2C19.
Specific ART interactions (PI-boosted raises atorvastatin, efavirenz lowers it): UNVERIFIED.** I did not check the Liverpool database. This is standard pharmacology and plausible.

Statin label warnings for liver disease and pregnancy: PLAUSIBLE but possibly outdated.** I did not search this. From background knowledge, FDA labelling was revised after 2012 to drop routine periodic LFT monitoring. The pregnancy contraindication was also relaxed in 2021. The "mandated LFT monitoring" scenario is therefore weaker than the critique implies.
Exclusion of 10–20% of adults, bringing 0.60 to 0.45–0.50: UNVERIFIABLE.** The Investigator labelled it illustrative and ungrounded. I found no data.
Many NTPs do not routinely perform LFTs in DS-TB: PLAUSIBLE.** I found no direct source. WHO guidance recommends symptom-based monitoring for most patients, which is consistent with it.
revised_hypothesis:
Anti-TB DILI is common, with a pooled incidence of about 11.5% and a range of roughly 2–28% or more. Clinicians may be reluctant to add a hepatically relevant agent that confounds attribution. Some eligibility exclusion (liver disease, pregnancy, polypharmacy) is therefore plausible. The cited drug-interaction concerns apply to CYP3A4-metabolised statins such as atorvastatin, not necessarily to pravastatin, which is the statin in the Phase 2b trial. The specific 0.45–0.50 figure is **UNGROUNDED — plausible but needs empirical support.** **Magnitude: low-to-medium.** Direction: decreases.

---
core_claim: Eligibility exclusions, DILI-attribution concerns and monitoring requirements would cut adult uptake from about 0.60 to about 0.45–0.50.
core_claim_reason: The mechanisms are plausible and the DILI base rate is verified, but I found no evidence for the size of the exclusion or program-reluctance effect.

original.thread_name: Implementation — trial execution, guideline adoption pathway,
original.title: Private-sector treatment share and the reach of national guidelines are not modeled
original.hypothesis: A large fraction of DS-TB treatment, especially in India, Indonesia, Pakistan and the Philippines, occurs in the private sector. Private providers frequently deviate from national standard treatment guidelines and may not use FDCs. Whether a WHO recommendation changes behavior there depends on professional societies, pharma marketing and mandatory notification, not on NTP procurement. Also, unnotified patients ("missing" cases, a large share in the same countries) never see the guideline. The relevant denominator for "60% of adult patients" is therefore a mix of settings with very different uptake dynamics.
original.mechanism: The effect on adult_uptake is ambiguous in sign. Private providers readily prescribe adjuncts and may adopt a cheap generic faster than NTPs, or even before guidelines (which would also reduce the counterfactual value of the trial). But dosing and duration there are unsupervised and non-standard, so effective exposure and benefit are lower. Net effect on the global average: probably a modest downward adjustment to effective uptake in the highest-burden countries, plausibly ~5–15% of the benefit. This is inference, not sourced. The sign could flip in specific countries.
suggested_evidence: WHO Global TB Reports contain country-level notification data and, I believe, India's Ni-kshay data show private-sector notifications of roughly a third of the total in recent years, but I cannot give exact figures. UNGROUNDED as to numbers. The claim that private-sector prescribing deviates from guidelines is widely discussed in the TB literature, but I cannot cite a specific paper.

evidence_found: Private practitioners in India have had to notify every TB case since a 2012 Gazette notification.
The mandatory-notification lever the critique mentions exists, but enforcement is weak.
Notification and public-health actions in the private sector have not really become routine practice.
The direction is ambiguous, as the critique admits. Rising private-sector linkage to NTP drugs argues against a net downward adjustment in India.
caveats: India's private-sector notifications are roughly a third of the total.* **VERIFIED.**
India's Ministry of Health reports 0.73 million private notifications in 2022 (30% of the total) and 0.83 million in 2023 (32%).
Other sources give
A large share of TB care is in the private sector in India, Indonesia, Pakistan and the Philippines.* **PARTIALLY VERIFIED.**
For India, a prevalence survey found about 50% of people with TB symptoms consult private facilities . This is much larger than the one-third notified share.
India, Indonesia, the Philippines and Pakistan are among the five countries with the most cases .
I found no data on private-sector share for Indonesia, Pakistan or the Philippines.
Private providers deviate from guidelines.* **PLAUSIBLE.**
Reports describe persistent underreporting, delays in diagnosis and treatment initiation, and weak adherence to standards of care in the Indian private sector.
I found no direct evidence on FDC use or dosing.
Unnotified ("missing") cases are a large share in the same countries.* **PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED for India.**
India cut missed notifications from 1.2 million in 2015 to 0.3 million in 2023.
Globally, notifications reached 78% of estimated incident cases .
The "large share missing" claim is therefore weaker for India than the critique implies. I did not check the other three countries.

Uptake depends on professional societies, pharma marketing and notification, not on NTP procurement.* **PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED.** India's programme is actively routing private patients to government supply.
Private-sector engagement agencies (PPSAs) link private patients to free public drugs and diagnostics.
The programme also works with professional bodies such as the Indian Medical Association.
Private-sector uptake therefore runs partly through NTP channels.
Net effect is a downward adjustment of about 5–15% of benefit.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** The critique itself labels this inference.
revised_hypothesis:
The private sector handles about one-third of notified cases in India. The share of all care-seeking is higher, with roughly half of symptomatic people consulting private providers. A guideline's reach into the private sector depends partly on notification mandates and PPSA-mediated access to free drugs. The model's single uptake figure does not capture this. The direction and size of the effect are **UNGROUNDED, plausible but needing empirical support**. Do not assert the 5–15% figure. Strength: **low–medium**, and the direction is uncertain, not "decreases".

---
core_claim: Effective uptake of a new regimen in the private sector is materially lower than the model assumes, giving a net downward adjustment to benefit.
core_claim_reason: The private share is real, but I found no evidence on private-sector uptake of new regimens, and the sign is admittedly ambiguous.

original.thread_name: Implementation — trial execution, guideline adoption pathway,
original.title: Zero modeled lag between Phase III completion and adoption, and a speedup that assumes trial timing is the binding constraint
original.hypothesis: The model treats years_to_adoption as equal to Phase III completion (8 years). Real-world chains include publication, WHO GDG convening and guideline development, national guideline revision, training, and GDF/Global Fund procurement cycles. For the 4-month HPMZ regimen, my recollection is that Study 31/A5349 published in 2021 and WHO guidance followed in 2022. The WHO step can therefore be short when a rapid-communication path is used. National adoption and procurement then took additional years. Separately, the 8-year timeline itself is exposed to execution risk. TB trials, particularly those run at multiple high-burden sites with a relapse endpoint requiring 12–24 months of follow-up, routinely slip. A generic drug also has no commercial sponsor, so Phase III funding could be a gating constraint, not the Phase IIc result. If so, a 1-year acceleration of the Phase IIc does not translate one-for-one into a 1-year earlier adoption.
original.mechanism: A longer years_to_adoption lowers eligible cases by ~2% per year under the current formula, which is not material alone (adding 3–5 years of lag lowers benefits by roughly 6–10%, more with discounting; see Thread 3). The larger concern is that expected speedup_years may be below 1 if the trial is not on the critical path. I note that lumpy decision cycles by themselves do not lower the expected speedup (if the timing is uniformly random, the expected shift equals the trial shift), so the case for a lower speedup rests on the trial not being the binding constraint, not on lumpiness.
suggested_evidence: Partly my recollection of the HPMZ timeline (verify). For Xpert, WHO endorsement was in 2010, and implementation took many years afterward (Albert et al., Cazabon et al. are the sources the thread names; I have not confirmed their specific findings). The Phase III funding-gap argument is a logical inference. Phase IIc registry timelines are not something I can cite.

evidence_found: The HPMZ case shows the WHO step can be very short once data exist. The critique's central point is that country adoption and the trial's place on the critical path matter more, which this case does not contradict. I found no HPMZ country-uptake data.
caveats: Real-world chains include long national adoption and procurement lags.* **PLAUSIBLE.** Xpert supports it. Early WHO endorsement was followed by a trial (registered 2013) describing Xpert as not yet integrated into national programmes .
A generic drug has no sponsor, so Phase III funding could gate the timeline.* **UNVERIFIABLE (logic).**
Phase III trials routinely slip.* **PLAUSIBLE.** No source was retrieved.
The model sets years_to_adoption equal to Phase III completion and loses about 2% of benefit per year of delay.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** I have no access to the model.
revised_hypothesis:
Correct the HPMZ chronology: WHO acted within weeks of publication in 2021, with consolidated guidelines in 2022. Retain the argument that post-guideline national adoption and procurement add lag, with Xpert as a qualitative analogy. Flag the Phase III funding gate and the claim that speedup is below 1 year as **UNGROUNDED**. The critique's own admission that lumpiness does not lower expected speedup should stay. Strength: **low–medium**.

---
core_claim: A 1-year acceleration of Phase IIc does not give a 1-year earlier adoption, because the trial is not the binding constraint.
core_claim_reason: Plausible, since sponsorship and funding could gate Phase III, but I found no evidence on this regimen's funding path or timeline.

original.thread_name: Who dies and how many healthy years are lost —
original.title: Survivors' excess mortality and comorbidity shrink the 27 DALYs per death
original.hypothesis: CG describes 27 as the "remaining healthy life expectancy" of a person who dies of TB. A person whose death is averted is not an average member of the population. TB patients carry high rates of smoking, alcohol use, diabetes, undernutrition, HIV and post-TB lung damage. Their expected remaining life after cure is therefore shorter than a general-population life table implies. If 27 comes from general-population or GBD-style life tables, it overstates the years gained per death averted.
original.mechanism:
dalys_per_death falls. Illustrative calculation (my own inference, not from a source):
- Under Gompertz mortality, multiplying the hazard by a factor k is roughly equivalent to ageing by ln(k)/b years. For b ≈ 0.09–0.10 per year and an SMR of about 3, that is ln(3)/0.09 ≈ 11–12 years of effective ageing.
- For a patient aged about 40, remaining life expectancy in an LMIC life table is roughly low-to-mid 30s. For an effective age of about 52 it is mid-20s.
- That is a 20–30% reduction in remaining life expectancy. 27 would fall to roughly 19–22, which is near or below the 17.7 threshold once combined with any other downward adjustment.
- The shift is partly offset if 27 is already a healthy-life measure built from a TB-specific population. It is amplified if CG took general-population HALE and then applied it unadjusted.
suggested_evidence: Romanowski et al. 2019 (Lancet Infect Dis), a systematic review of long-term all-cause mortality after TB treatment. I recall a pooled SMR of roughly 3–4 versus general populations, but the exact figure needs verification.
Gompertz scaling is a standard demographic approximation.
The SMR is partly confounded by shared risk factors. That is exactly why the counterfactual years of an averted-death patient are lower than the population average.
I cannot identify a source for how CG derived 27.

evidence_found: Independent support:
A lifetime-burden analysis estimated 12.1 DALYs per incident TB case, 5.8 of them from post-TB sequelae .
Per-case post-TB burden was greater for younger people and in high-incidence countries.
This confirms that post-TB morbidity and mortality are material. It also shows that burden estimates can include post-TB effects, which could offset the critique if CG's figure already includes them.

A large 2026 cohort comparison found elevated natural-cause mortality in the treated cohort (RR = 1.77) . This is lower than Romanowski's pooled estimate, which suggests k = 3 may be on the high side.
Using k ≈ 1.8 instead of 2.9 gives an effective ageing of about 6.5 years, which roughly halves the reduction the critique computes.
caveats: The Gompertz shift is ln(k)/b, which is about 11–12 years for k = 3 and b = 0.09.* **VERIFIED (arithmetic).** With the real estimate of 2.91, ln(2.91)/0.09 ≈ 11.9 years.
Remaining life expectancy at 40 is low-to-mid 30s, and in the mid-20s at effective age 52.* **PLAUSIBLE.** I did not retrieve a life table.
That implies a 20–30% reduction, so 27 falls to about 19–22.* **PLAUSIBLE but conditional.**
It holds only if 27 came from an unadjusted general-population table.
The SMR is also confounded, as the critique notes. For a counterfactual averted-death patient, shared risk factors still apply.
A first-year or on-treatment death averted differs from a post-treatment survivor, so applying the post-treatment SMR to the whole remaining lifespan is a modelling choice.
The 17.7 threshold.* **UNVERIFIABLE.** It comes from the model I cannot see.
CG's derivation of 27.* **UNVERIFIABLE.
revised_hypothesis: Survivors of TB have roughly 1.8–2.9 times the all-cause mortality of the general population, per Romanowski 2019 (2.91, 95% CI 2.21–3.84) and a recent cohort study (RR 1.77). Applying general-population life expectancy to averted deaths probably overstates years gained. Using Gompertz scaling, the plausible reduction is about 10–25%, not a flat 20–30%, and it is **conditional on the provenance of 27**, which is **UNGROUNDED**. The claim that 27 falls "near or below 17.7" is a model-specific inference. Strength: **medium**, down from large, until the source of 27 is known.
core_claim: The 27 DALYs per death derives from general-population or GBD-style life tables and is therefore overstated for the people whose deaths are actually averted.
core_claim_reason: Excess post-TB mortality is well documented, but I could not find how CG built 27. It may already be a TB-specific or healthy-life figure, which would offset the adjustment.

original.thread_name: Who dies and how many healthy years are lost —
original.title: The 6% is a mix of deaths, and only a fraction is reachable and modifiable by atorvastatin
original.hypothesis: On-treatment deaths are concentrated early. Many occur in the first weeks, often in patients who are very sick, severely malnourished, or have advanced HIV, and some occur before or just after treatment initiation. A host-directed adjunct that takes time to reach effective exposure, and is further limited by rifampicin induction, cannot avert deaths that occur within days. Some deaths are also non-TB causes (HIV-related, cardiovascular, hepatic, or other). The "addressable" share of the 6% is therefore smaller than 6%.
original.mechanism:
This is a decomposition of baseline_mortality into an effective baseline, addressable_mortality = 6% × (share of deaths occurring after statin could plausibly act) × (share TB-attributable and statin-responsive) × (share of the population eligible for statin).
- Illustrative only: if 30% of deaths are very early or in contraindicated or sicker-than-eligible groups, and 15% are non-TB causes, effective baseline is 6% × 0.7 × 0.85 ≈ 3.6%. That is below the 3.9% threshold.
- These shares are placeholders. I do not have verified values.
suggested_evidence: Waitt & Squire 2011 (IJTLD), a systematic review of risk factors for death during and after TB treatment. I believe it reports HIV, older age, and malnutrition as risk factors and that many deaths occur early, but details need verification.
Country cohort studies (India, South Africa, Indonesia, Nigeria) on timing of death. I cannot cite specific ones.
The rifampicin–atorvastatin interaction is pharmacologically established. Its effect on onset of benefit is an inference.

evidence_found: The timing evidence above comes from Zambia, Kenya, Ethiopia, Turkey, Cameroon and India. It supports the early-death premise strongly.

Caveat the Investigator did not raise: if the model's statin effect size comes from a trial population, it already excludes very early or ineligible deaths. Applying the "addressable share" haircut on top would double-count.
The eligibility factor appears in the mechanism formula but not in the worked example.
Early deaths may be partly reversible with timely care.
Deaths within 14 days of anti-TB treatment suggest some mortality may have been reversible with earlier therapy.
That cuts against treating all very early deaths as unreachable.
caveats: Deaths are concentrated early, in the first weeks: **VERIFIED.**
Zambia, 1,063 deaths:
58.1% occurred in the first month and 75.1% in the first two months.
The median time to death was 21 days.
Kenya, Meru County:
76% of deaths occurred within three months of starting treatment.
Ethiopia:
More than 70% of deaths occur in the first two months.
Taiwan:
Underweight was associated with higher mortality only in the first 8 weeks.
Very sick, malnourished or advanced-HIV patients dominate early deaths: **VERIFIED.**
The major risk factors for early death are HIV positivity, old age, being underweight and retreatment.
Some deaths are non-TB causes: **VERIFIED.** A Taiwanese review classified deaths as TB-related or non-TB-related.
Most TB-related deaths occurred early, with a median survival of 20 days.
The non-TB share varies by setting, and I did not find a pooled figure.
Some deaths occur before treatment starts: **VERIFIED, but outside the treated cohort.** In a US study,
TB-related death occurred during treatment for 75% of decedents and before treatment began for 25%.
These deaths would not be in an on-treatment 6%.
Rifampicin induction delays onset of statin benefit: **PLAUSIBLE.** The interaction is real. The timing of induction relative to benefit is an inference, and the Investigator labels it as one.
The arithmetic 6% × 0.7 × 0.85 = 3.57%: **VERIFIED** (≈3.6%). I could not verify the 3.9% threshold. It comes from the source model.
The 30% and 15% shares are placeholders, as the Investigator says. The 30% is plausible for deaths within about 2 weeks, given the Zambian median of 21 days. The 15% non-TB share is unsupported.
revised_hypothesis:
- Deaths during TB treatment are heavily front-loaded. In several African cohorts, roughly 55–75% occur within 1–2 months, and the median is about 3 weeks in Zambia.
- Early deaths are concentrated in HIV-positive, underweight and older patients. Rifampicin cuts atorvastatin exposure substantially.
- Applying the 6% to all patients probably overstates the share a statin could avert.
- **UNGROUNDED:** the size of the haircut. Needed evidence: statin time-to-effect, the TB-attributable share of deaths, and whether the model's effect size already reflects an enrolled trial population.
- Strength: medium, direction decreases, with a caution against double-counting.

---
core_claim: A large enough share of the 6% is unreachable or non-TB (about 35–40% combined) to push the effective baseline below 3.9%.
core_claim_reason: Early concentration of deaths is directly supported, but the specific shares are acknowledged placeholders, and I found no evidence on the statin onset-time or non-TB share needed to reach the threshold.

original.thread_name: Who dies and how many healthy years are lost —
original.title: Under-ascertained deaths push true mortality up, and the direction is the opposite of Critiques 1–2
original.hypothesis: The 6% appears to come from the "died" category of WHO notified-cohort outcomes. That category excludes deaths among patients lost to follow-up (typically ~3–4% of the cohort), those "not evaluated" (a few percent), and deaths before treatment start or among transferred-out patients. It also excludes deaths among untreated or un-notified cases, who are unreachable for statin delivery but not for the all-in cost-effectiveness logic. If a meaningful share of LTFU and not-evaluated patients die, true on-treatment mortality among treated patients is above 6%.
original.mechanism:
baseline_mortality rises.
- Illustrative arithmetic: if LTFU plus not-evaluated is about 6–7% of the cohort and 10–20% of them die, that adds roughly 0.6–1.4 percentage points. True mortality is then about 6.6–7.4%, which raises SROI by roughly 10–23% (proportional to mortality).
- The caveat is that the statin effect on those patients is uncertain, because they may not complete treatment.
suggested_evidence: The WHO Global TB Report outcome tables define treatment outcomes this way. I recall about 5–6% died, ~3–4% LTFU, and a few percent not evaluated, but the figures need checking.
I believe tracing studies of patients lost to follow-up show materially elevated mortality, but I cannot identify a specific study. UNGROUNDED on magnitude.

evidence_found: Mortality in some settings is already above 6%, for example
8.6% among South African adults on treatment.
This shows that 6% is a global average, not a floor.

A conceptual weakness: many LTFU deaths happen after treatment stops. They are not on-treatment deaths, so a statin taken during treatment may not be able to avert them. The Investigator mentions this caveat but still applies the full proportional uplift to SROI.

"Not evaluated" includes transfers and missing records, and most of these patients are probably alive. A 10–20% death rate for that group is unsupported. The 10–20% range fits LTFU better than the not-evaluated group.
This critique and Critique 1 pull in opposite directions. Both are plausible, and the net effect is undetermined.
caveats: The 6% comes from the "died" category and excludes LTFU and not-evaluated patients: **PLAUSIBLE.** WHO's definition supports the structure. I cannot confirm how the source model derived its 6%.
LTFU is about 3–4% and not-evaluated a few percent: **PLAUSIBLE.**
Uganda/Kenya-type cohort:
5.5% died and 2.6% were LTFU , and 618/10,717 (5.8%) were not evaluated.
Kenya, Meru County:
6.3% were LTFU and 5.1% died.
Ranges vary widely by country, and Zimbabwe has very high not-evaluated shares.
A meaningful share of LTFU patients die: **SUPPORTED for TB, at the low end of the Investigator's 10–20%.**
Kenya CHP tracing: of 140 patients identified for tracing, 36 (25.7%) were traced, 90 had relocated and 14 (10.0%) had died.
A medRxiv cohort found that
LTFU raised standardized five-year mortality by 2.23 percentage points.
It noted that
SMRs after LTFU are two to seven times higher than after cure.
Cape Town tracing: a small share died among true LTFU (1/30 and 3/12 in two subgroups). That is a low and noisy signal.
The HIV ART LTFU meta-analysis (20–60% of traced patients dead) is about ART programmes, not TB, so it should not be used for the TB range.
Pre-treatment deaths and untreated cases are excluded: **VERIFIED, but not statin-reachable.** In Zimbabwe,
49.6% (252/508) of pre-treatment lost-to-follow-up TB patients died. In Cape Town,
2% died before starting treatment.
The title says "opposite of Critiques 1–2", but this is Critique 2. It is probably a labelling slip and should say "opposite of Critique 1".
revised_hypothesis:
- WHO outcome categories exclude post-LTFU and pre-treatment deaths. TB-specific evidence shows elevated mortality among LTFU patients, with about 10% found dead in one Kenyan tracing study and SMRs 2–7× higher than after cure.
- True all-cause mortality among everyone who starts treatment is therefore probably somewhat above the "died" category.
- The SROI uplift is smaller than 10–23% if the statin cannot affect deaths after treatment interruption.
- **UNGROUNDED:** the exact WHO shares and the 10–20% death rate for not-evaluated patients.
- Strength: low-to-medium, direction increases. Reduce the weight because of the addressability caveat.

---
core_claim: A meaningful share of LTFU and not-evaluated patients die, so true mortality among treated patients exceeds 6%, and the excess is relevant to statin benefit.
core_claim_reason: Tracing and cohort data show elevated post-LTFU mortality (about 10% in Kenya, SMR 2–7×), but no source shows these deaths are modifiable by an adjunct taken during treatment.

original.thread_name: Who dies and how many healthy years are lost —
original.title: Covariance between mortality and DALYs per death means the product of means is not the mean of the product
original.hypothesis: baseline_mortality and dalys_per_death are applied as independent averages. In reality the subgroups with the highest mortality (older, comorbid, advanced disease) tend to have fewer remaining years. Groups with lower mortality are younger, with more years lost per death. The relevant quantity is the death-weighted mean DALYs, not the population mean. If 27 was derived without that weighting, the product 6% × 27 is biased. HIV-positive deaths push the other way, since they occur at younger ages and carry more DALYs per death.
original.mechanism:
Illustrative arithmetic (my own, assumed numbers):
- Group A is 70% of patients, with 4% mortality and 35 DALYs per death. Group B is 30% of patients, with 12% mortality and 15 DALYs per death.
- Mean mortality is 6.4%. Death-weighted DALYs are (0.028×35 + 0.036×15)/0.064 ≈ 23.8, not 27.
- Expected DALYs per treated patient is 1.52, versus 6.4% × 27 = 1.73 if the population-average 27 is used. That is about 12% lower.
- The effect could be near zero or reversed if HIV+ deaths dominate in high-HIV deployment settings.
- Conclusion: the net effect on SROI is uncertain in sign but plausibly −10 to −15% in low-HIV settings.
suggested_evidence: GBD 2021 TB deaths and YLLs by age, country and HIV status could be used to compute death-weighted YLL per death. I have not run this, and it needs verification.
The structure of the bias is a logical argument.
The group numbers above are illustrative, not sourced.

evidence_found: Two points weaken the critique:
Statin benefit may not be proportional across subgroups, so the right weight is deaths averted, not deaths.
The Investigator concedes the sign is uncertain, particularly in high-HIV settings. The stated direction "decreases" with a −10 to −15% range is therefore stronger than the evidence allows.
The critique's structural point (E[m·d] ≠ E[m]·E[d] when the two covary) is mathematically correct.
caveats: The arithmetic is **VERIFIED:**
Expected DALYs per patient = 1.52, versus 6.4%×27 = 1.73, which is −12%.

The illustrative inputs are internally inconsistent with the "27" baseline. The case-weighted mean of 35 and 15 is 0.7×35 + 0.3×15 = 29, not 27. If 29 were the population-average comparator, the bias would be −18%, not −12%.
Higher mortality in older or comorbid patients: **VERIFIED.**
Advanced age raised the risk of death during treatment in Turkey.
Old age, TB/HIV co-infection and baseline body weight under 35 kg increased mortality in Ethiopia.
HIV deaths push the other way: **PLAUSIBLE and consistent with the evidence.** In Cape Town, the main risk factor was HIV status at treatment start.
HIV-associated deaths tend to be in younger adults. I did not retrieve an age-specific YLL figure.

"27 was derived without death-weighting": **UNVERIFIABLE.** I do not know how 27 was derived. If it came from GBD YLL ÷ deaths, it is already death-weighted by construction, and the critique's concern would not apply. The critique matters only if 27 came from a population or case-weighted age-at-diagnosis calculation.
revised_hypothesis:
- If dalys_per_death is a case-weighted or population-average figure rather than a death-weighted one, multiplying it by mean mortality can misstate expected DALYs averted.
- Age is a known mortality risk factor, which supports a negative covariance in low-HIV settings. HIV-associated deaths in younger adults push the other way, so the net sign is uncertain.
- **UNGROUNDED:** the −10 to −15% magnitude. It depends on how 27 was derived and on GBD age- and HIV-stratified YLL data.
- Check first whether 27 is already GBD YLL ÷ deaths. If so, drop this critique.
- Strength: low-to-medium, direction uncertain (lean decreases in low-HIV settings only).
core_claim: The 27 DALYs/death input is not death-weighted, and the covariance is negative enough to bias the product upward by about 10–15%.
core_claim_reason: The covariance logic is sound, but I found no evidence on how 27 was derived or on the actual size of the covariance.

original.thread_name: Who dies and how many healthy years are lost —
original.title: A global-average mortality may not match the countries where an atorvastatin adjunct would actually be deployed
original.hypothesis: baseline_mortality is a single global figure, but on-treatment mortality varies a lot by country, mainly through HIV prevalence, age mix, and diagnostic delay. The Phase III trials and eventual uptake would concentrate in a handful of high-burden countries (e.g., India, South Africa, Indonesia, Nigeria, Philippines). If deployment is weighted toward lower-mortality settings, the 6% overstates. If weighted toward high-HIV settings, it understates and the DALYs per death shift too.
original.mechanism: baseline_mortality becomes a case-weighted average over deployment countries rather than the global figure. If India (a large share of cases) has on-treatment death near 4–5% and South Africa near 8–10% (both from memory, UNVERIFIED), the weighted mean depends heavily on the deployment mix. A mix dominated by India could bring the figure to about 4.5%, still above the 3.9% threshold. A mix dominated by high-HIV countries would exceed 6%. This is a sensitivity issue rather than a clear bias.
suggested_evidence: WHO Global TB Report country-level outcome data for the 2021 or 2022 cohorts.
GBD country-level TB deaths and YLLs.
I cannot cite country-specific figures with confidence. UNGROUNDED.

evidence_found: WHO reports a sustained high treatment success rate for drug-susceptible TB, 88% globally in 2023 and 2022 . The residual 12% (deaths, loss to follow-up, failure) leaves room for substantial country spread.

One caveat the critique misses: trial-enrolled patients usually have lower on-treatment mortality than programmatic cohorts. The relevant baseline for a Phase III-based effect may be below WHO country figures. That would push the number down in every country.
caveats: TB burden is concentrated in India, Indonesia, the Philippines, Nigeria and South Africa: VERIFIED.** The CDC/WHO 2019 summary lists

India (26%), Indonesia (8.5%), China (8.4%), the Philippines (6.0%), Pakistan (5.7%), Nigeria (4.4%), Bangladesh (3.6%), and South Africa (3.6%) as the eight countries with two thirds of global cases.
On-treatment mortality differs by country: PLAUSIBLE.** A model-based analysis of Brazil, India and South Africa reports different deviations in deaths during treatment in each country (
13.7% higher than predicted in Brazil, 1.7% in India and 21.8% in South Africa
). That shows heterogeneity in how deaths changed, not baseline levels.

India about 4–5% and South Africa about 8–10%: UNVERIFIABLE.** The critique itself flags these as from memory. My searches did not return the WHO country-level cohort tables. An Indian systematic review of treatment-phase case fatality exists (
India accounts for a third of global TB deaths; the review covers cohort studies and trial control arms
). I did not retrieve its pooled estimate.

The global 6% figure, the 3.9% threshold and the "Phase III and uptake concentrate in a handful of countries" claim: UNVERIFIABLE.** These are properties of the model or its deployment plan, which I could not check.
revised_hypothesis:
Baseline mortality is a global figure, but TB burden is concentrated in a few countries whose on-treatment mortality probably differs (HIV, age mix, delay to diagnosis). The model should show a case-weighted sensitivity range. Remove the specific India and South Africa percentages until sourced from WHO country cohort tables. Also consider trial-versus-programme mortality differences. Direction: uncertain. Magnitude: medium-low. Strength: moderate-weak.

---
core_claim: Country-weighted on-treatment mortality could differ materially from the single global 6% figure, depending on deployment mix.
core_claim_reason: Heterogeneity is plausible and directionally supported, but I found no country-specific on-treatment death percentages to size it.

original.thread_name: Probability of success (p_success) — base rates and the
original.title: Industry phase-transition base rates put "II and III both succeed" at roughly 15–25%, so 40% requires an unstated premium of about 1.6–2.7×
original.hypothesis: CG names no reference class for 40%. The best-known class is industry phase-transition data. From memory, BIO/Informa/QLS (2021, covering 2011–2020) report about 29% for Phase II→III, about 58% for Phase III→NDA/BLA, and about 91% for filing→approval. Wong, Siah & Lo (2019, *Biostatistics*) give similar overall figures, with infectious-disease or anti-infective programs doing better than average. On these numbers, P(II and III both succeed) is about 0.29 × 0.58 ≈ 17%, and P(II→approval) is about 15%. Even generously uplifted for infectious disease (say Phase II ~37–40% and Phase III ~65%), the product is about 24–26%. That is at or below the 0.26 break-even. To justify 40%, CG needs a premium of roughly 1.6× over the infectious-disease-adjusted rate, or about 2.4× over the all-indication rate. The model never states or defends that premium.
original.mechanism:
p_success enters linearly. A move from 0.40 to 0.20–0.25 cuts expected cost-effectiveness by 37–50%. This crosses the 0.26 threshold, below which SROI falls under the bar. A proposed decomposition, with the reasoning shown:
- P(IIc success) ≈ 0.5. This is higher than the 29–40% industry Phase II rate because a PK/dose-selection Phase IIc is easier to "pass".
- P(III | IIc) ≈ 0.40–0.55, adjusted for infectious disease and repurposing but not for the TB-specific track record (Critique 2).
- P(adopted | III) ≈ 0.7–0.85 (Critique 4).
- Product ≈ 0.14–0.30, with a central value of about 0.20.

This decomposition is my own inference, not from a source.
suggested_evidence: Published industry datasets (BIO/Informa/QLS 2021; Wong, Siah & Lo 2019). Figures are from memory and should be verified, especially the infectious-disease-specific rates. A counter-argument CG could make is that repurposed or generic drugs have known safety, which lifts Phase I and II transition rates. I believe the literature supports some premium, but I cannot cite a specific source for the size of a repurposing premium. That is UNGROUNDED. The premium mostly applies to safety attrition, whereas the dominant failure mode in Phase II/III is lack of efficacy, which repurposing does not help.

evidence_found: Hay et al. 2014 (via a secondary source) put the non-oncology Phase II→III rate at 34.8% and Phase III success at 54% . This corroborates the general range.

Industry transition rates measure drug progression, which includes business-driven terminations. They may understate the scientific probability of success for a well-funded academic or public-health program. They are also not defined identically to CG's p_success, which may start at Phase IIc and end at adoption. The critique doesn't discuss this definitional mismatch.
The critique's internal cross-references ("Critique 2", "Critique 4") do not match this batch's numbering.
caveats: Phase II→III about 29%: VERIFIED.** BIO's figure is 28.9% .
Phase III→NDA/BLA about 58%: VERIFIED.** The BIO table gives 57.8% for Phase III.
Filing→approval about 91%: UNVERIFIABLE** in my results, though plausible.
Arithmetic: VERIFIED.** 0.289 × 0.578 ≈ 16.7%. The 1.6×–2.7× premium and the 37–50% cut from moving 0.40 to 0.20–0.25 are correct.
Infectious-disease uplift gives Phase III about 65% and a product of 24–26%: PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED.**
One analysis of a different dataset finds infectious diseases have the highest unconditional success rate at 14.0%, with a Phase III success rate of 80.9% and application success of 95.6% .
This is a different methodology from BIO and probably uses different phase definitions. Still, it suggests the critique's assumed 65% Phase III rate for infectious disease may be too low.
With Phase II at about 37–40% and Phase III at about 80%, the product is roughly 30%, not 24–26%.
It would still be below 40%, but near the 0.26 break-even. The critique's central 0.20 looks somewhat pessimistic.

Anti-infective overall rates are not dramatically above average: VERIFIED.** Anti-infective Phase I→approval is fairly stable around 10.6% . Wong et al. report that only 6.8% of non-industry-sponsored vaccine and 8.2% of non-vaccine infectious-disease programs transition from phase 1 to approval . This mildly supports the critique's skepticism.
Repurposing premium applies mostly to safety attrition, not efficacy: LOGIC ONLY.** The critique flags this as UNGROUNDED, which is accurate.
The PIIc success estimate of 0.5 and the decomposition: UNVERIFIABLE** (own inference, as stated).
The 0.26 break-even and CG's 40%: UNVERIFIABLE.** They come from the model.
revised_hypothesis:
CG gives no reference class for 40%. BIO 2011–2020 rates (Phase II→III 28.9%, Phase III→filing 57.8%) imply about 17% for both phases. Infectious-disease-specific data (one analysis: Phase III about 81%) lift this to roughly 25–32%, which is still below 40% and close to the 0.26 break-even. Remove the claim that the infectious-disease-adjusted product is 24–26%. Replace it with a range of about 25–32%, and state that the Wong 2019 figures need checking against the corrected tables. The own-inference decomposition is UNGROUNDED. The repurposing-premium argument is plausible but unsourced. Strength: moderate-to-strong on direction, with the size of the gap uncertain. Magnitude: medium-large.

---
core_claim: Industry reference-class rates imply P(II and III succeed) of roughly 15–25%, so CG's 40% needs an unstated premium of about 1.6× or more.
core_claim_reason: The BIO rates were directly confirmed, but the infectious-disease uplift could be larger than assumed and CG's endpoint definition is unknown.

original.thread_name: Probability of success (p_success) — base rates and the
original.title: The TB-specific reference classes (host-directed therapy, adjunctives, regimen-shortening) have a much worse record than 40%
original.hypothesis:
The relevant class is not "drugs" but "TB host-directed or adjunctive therapies, and TB treatment-shortening strategies promoted on animal or early-phase surrogate data". To my knowledge this class has a poor Phase III record.
- **Vitamin D.** Trials in Guinea-Bissau (Wejse et al., 2009) and London (Martineau et al., 2011) showed no mortality or overall culture-conversion benefit. I am fairly confident of this but have not checked details.
- **Fluoroquinolone 4-month regimens.** REMoxTB, OFLOTUB and RIFAQUIN failed non-inferiority in Phase III despite encouraging mouse and Phase II (culture-conversion) data. This is the closest analogue to "promising preclinical plus Phase II surrogate → Phase III".
- **Dexamethasone in HIV-associated TB meningitis.** The ACT HIV trial (2023) was, as I recall, null on survival. This is a case where an adjunctive anti-inflammatory looked effective in an earlier trial population and did not generalize.
- **Corticosteroids.** These are the counter-example: benefit in TB meningitis (Thwaites 2004) and pericarditis, and they were adopted. They are the one clear success of the class.
- **Other HDTs.** Statins, metformin and others have mostly mouse and observational support. To my knowledge no HDT is WHO-recommended for drug-sensitive pulmonary TB. Reviews such as Wallis & Hafner and Kolloli & Subbian describe a pipeline that is mostly preclinical or small Phase II.
- **Statin preclinical data.** Mouse data for pravastatin (Parihar and colleagues, Karakousis group) are promising. Observational human data (statin use and lower TB risk) are subject to healthy-user bias.

A success rate for this class of well under 40% from Phase II onward looks plausible, perhaps 10–20%. However, Study 31/A5349 (rifapentine-moxifloxacin 4-month regimen) succeeded and was adopted, so the class is not zero.
original.mechanism: Using the TB-class prior in place of the generic one gives p_success of roughly 0.10–0.25 (my inference). At 0.15, cost-effectiveness is about 38% of the CG base case, well below the bar. Even a blend of the TB-class and industry priors gives p_success ≈ 0.2–0.3.
suggested_evidence: The cited trials are real as far as I recall, but exact results and endpoints need Verifier checking. The class-level success rate is my inference, not a published number. I cannot cite a systematic review giving a "HDT success rate for TB". UNGROUNDED as a quantitative rate.

evidence_found: A vitamin D meta-analysis found a significantly higher proportion of sputum culture conversion overall (OR 1.22, 1.04–1.43), but no shortening of time to conversion . This is a mild counterweight to "null."

The 2025 LAST ACT trial in HIV-negative adults, stratified by LTA4H genotype, found neither non-inferiority nor superiority of placebo established in CC/CT-genotype adults . A combined analysis supports dexamethasone's modest survival benefit in all HIV-negative adults . This reinforces that even the one adopted class member has a modest, heterogeneous effect.
Reference-class weakness:**
The list is a hand-picked set of failures, so it is vulnerable to selection bias.
Several trials were themselves Phase II/III, not Phase II→III transitions.
The ACT HIV trial concerned TB meningitis mortality, a very different setting from pulmonary TB with a culture-conversion or relapse endpoint.
Most statin evidence is preclinical, so a 10–20% rate from this class has no denominator.
caveats: "No HDT is WHO-recommended for drug-sensitive pulmonary TB": PLAUSIBLE, unchecked.**
Class success rate of 10–20%: UNVERIFIABLE** (own inference, as stated).
At p=0.15, cost-effectiveness is about 38% of CG's base case: VERIFIED arithmetically** (0.15/0.40 = 0.375).
revised_hypothesis: TB adjunctive and host-directed trials have a mixed record. Vitamin D showed no overall benefit on culture conversion (Wejse 2009, Martineau 2011). Dexamethasone in HIV-associated TB meningitis was null (ACT HIV, HR 0.85, 0.66–1.10). Dexamethasone in HIV-negative TB meningitis showed benefit (Thwaites 2004), though it is modest and heterogeneous. The fluoroquinolone 4-month failures and the Study 31 success are from the critique's memory and need a check. Remove the Parihar/Karakousis attribution until verified. The 10–20% class rate and the blended p_success of 0.2–0.3 are UNGROUNDED inferences. They are plausible, but the reference class is selective and the endpoint context differs from pulmonary TB. Direction: lowers p_success. Magnitude: medium-large. Strength: moderate, as a qualitative prior shift rather than a quantified one.
core_claim: The appropriate TB-specific reference class has a success rate well under 40% from Phase II onward (about 10–20%).
core_claim_reason: The individual trial facts check out, but the class rate is an unpublished inference built from a non-systematic, selected list.

original.thread_name: Probability of success (p_success) — base rates and the
original.title: "Success" probably means a surrogate or composite endpoint, but the model needs a 10% mortality reduction, so P(adopted AND 10% mortality benefit) < P(trials succeed)
original.hypothesis:
CG's p_success is defined as "Phase II and III both succeed", and the benefit is a 10% relative mortality reduction. A Phase III TB trial cannot realistically be powered to show a 10% relative mortality reduction.

A power calculation with reasoning shown (my own arithmetic):
- Assume baseline trial-population mortality of about 4% (programmatic mortality in DS-TB is of similar order, maybe 4–6%).
- A 10% relative reduction is 0.4 percentage points (4.0% → 3.6%).
- Using n ≈ (1.96 + 0.84)² × [p₁q₁ + p₂q₂] / d², n ≈ 7.84 × 0.0731 / (0.004)² ≈ 36,000 per arm, about 70,000 in total.
- Even at 6% baseline mortality, this is still tens of thousands per arm.

Standard TB Phase III trials enroll hundreds to a few thousand and use composite "unfavorable outcome", relapse or culture-conversion endpoints. So "Phase III success" will almost certainly be declared on a surrogate or composite endpoint. The 10% mortality figure is then an extrapolation never directly tested. P(trials succeed) overstates P(adopted AND mortality benefit ≥ 10%). The mortality benefit conditional on surrogate success is uncertain and could be much smaller.
original.mechanism: The model effectively computes p_success × uptake × 10% × deaths. The coherent quantity is P(trials succeed on surrogate) × P(adopted | success) × E[mortality reduction | surrogate success, adoption]. If E[RR | surrogate success] is 5–7% rather than 10%, benefit falls 30–50%, compounding with any p_success revision. The magnitude depends on the surrogate-to-mortality relationship, which is uncertain, so it needs a sensitivity analysis. Also note that if success needs a 10% mortality effect to be real, the true probability is lower still. Unless the success definition is aligned with the 10%, the two parameters cannot both be right.
suggested_evidence: Logical and arithmetic argument, based on standard sample-size mathematics. The baseline mortality is an assumption, so the Verifier should check typical DS-TB trial mortality rates and the primary endpoints of recent Phase III trials such as Study 31, REMoxTB and TRUNCATE-TB. The surrogate-to-mortality relationship for TB adjuncts is UNGROUNDED here.

evidence_found: Counter-consideration.** The critique's DS-TB framing may not match the model. In high-mortality populations such as TB meningitis or advanced HIV, mortality-powered trials are feasible. One review notes dexamethasone significantly reduces mortality in tuberculous meningitis and pericarditis.
If CG targets those populations, the power argument weakens.
Possible misreading of the 10%.** The model's 10% may be a population-level or assumed effect, not the trial's powered effect size. I could not see CG's model, so I could not check this.
caveats: Power calculation (~36,000 per arm at 4% → 3.6%): VERIFIED (arithmetic).** I recomputed it. The variance term is 0.0384 + 0.0347 = 0.0731. Then 7.84 × 0.0731 / 0.004² ≈ 35,800 per arm.
Baseline mortality of ~4% in trial populations: FALSE or overstated for trials, and the error makes the critique stronger.**
Study 31 on-treatment all-cause mortality was 0.8% (control), 0.4% (rifapentine–moxifloxacin) and 0.5% (rifapentine).
Overall mortality in Study 31 was 0.6%.
Among people with HIV it was 1.5%.
In TRUNCATE-TB, deaths before week 96 were 2 (1.1%) in the control arm and 5 (2.7%) in one experimental arm.
At about 1% baseline, my calculation gives roughly 148,000 per arm. The 4–6% figure is closer to programmatic cohorts, which I did not verify.
Standard Phase III TB trials use composite endpoints, not mortality: VERIFIED.**
Study 31's primary efficacy endpoint was TB disease-free survival at 12 months.
REMoxTB's primary endpoint was a composite unfavorable outcome (failure or relapse within 18 months).
TRUNCATE-TB's primary outcome was a composite of death before week 96, or ongoing treatment or active TB at week 96.
Another source says the accepted primary efficacy endpoint is a composite of mainly bacteriological failure and relapse.
Enrolment of "hundreds to a few thousand": VERIFIED.** Study 31 randomized about 2,500 and TRUNCATE-TB about 675 across its arms.
The surrogate-to-mortality link is uncertain: PLAUSIBLE.** Culture-conversion surrogates are known to be weak.
Culture conversion has only a limited role in advancing regimens to phase III or predicting outcomes.
That evidence concerns culture conversion and relapse, not mortality for adjunct drugs.
"E[RR | surrogate success] is 5–7%": UNGROUNDED.** It is an illustrative number with no source.
revised_hypothesis:
- **Verified:** A mortality-powered Phase III in a typical drug-susceptible TB population needs about 36,000 per arm at 4% baseline mortality. It would need far more at the 0.5–2% mortality seen in Study 31 and TRUNCATE-TB. Standard TB Phase III trials use composite unfavorable-outcome endpoints.
- **Implication:** If CG's population is DS-TB or similarly low-mortality, the 10% mortality effect is an extrapolation, and the model should state it separately from P(trial success).
- **Flagged:** The 5–7% discount is UNGROUNDED. The critique does not apply in high-mortality populations. CG's definition of success needs checking.
- **Strength:** Large if the population is low-mortality, but conditional on that. The direction is correct.

---
core_claim: CG's "Phase III success" is declared on a surrogate or composite endpoint that does not directly test a 10% mortality reduction, so P(success) overstates P(adopted AND ≥10% mortality benefit).
core_claim_reason: The arithmetic and TB endpoint conventions are verified, but I found no evidence on how CG defines success or on the actual mortality-conditional effect.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: Baseline year is stale and the 5.5M figure is sensitive to it
original.hypothesis: If CG anchored on 2022 notifications (~7.5M), that was a post-COVID recovery year. WHO's later reports show notifications continuing to rise (~8.2M in 2023). The "8 years of decline" is then applied from a baseline that is already out of date. The thread notes there is no sensitivity analysis on baseline year.
original.mechanism: Moving the baseline from 7.5M to ~8.2–8.3M raises eligible_people_at_8y by ~9–11%, from ~5.5M to ~6.0–6.1M. Taken alone this is below the ±25% materiality bar. It is an upward, non-material correction. It matters mainly because it stacks with Critique 2.
suggested_evidence: Logical argument plus my recollection of WHO Global TB Reports (2023 and 2024 editions). I cannot give exact figures. This is a reconstruction concern and would need verification against the WHO reports.

evidence_found: The 2025 WHO report is already out. It gives 2024 notifications as 8.3M, and notifications were 78% of estimated incidence . A baseline of 2023 or 2024 is therefore clearly available.
Notifications rose even though incidence was flat to slightly down, which is the detection-gap mechanism behind Critique 2.
caveats: 2022 notifications ≈ 7.5M:** VERIFIED.
