WHO reported about 8.2 million newly diagnosed in 2023, up from 7.5 million in 2022.
2023 ≈ 8.2M:** VERIFIED.
Globally in 2023, 8.2 million people with a new episode of TB were diagnosed and notified.
"Later reports show notifications continuing to rise" (8.3M for 2024):** VERIFIED, but the rise has flattened.
In 2024, 8.3 million were notified, similar to the 8.2 million in 2023 and 17% above the pre-pandemic 7.1 million in 2019.
The critique's "~8.2–8.3M" range is therefore accurate.
"2022 was a post-COVID recovery year":** VERIFIED.
WHO says those diagnosed in 2022 and 2023 probably included a sizeable backlog of people whose diagnosis was delayed by COVID.
The critique does not note that 2023 shares this backlog caveat. 2024 held at 8.3M, though, so the higher level looks persistent.

Uplift of 9–11% (5.5M → 6.0–6.1M):** VERIFIED arithmetic. 8.2/7.5 = +9.3% and 8.3/7.5 = +10.7%. The 5.5M figure also reconciles with 7.5M × 0.98⁸ × 0.96 × ~0.90, which suggests the model is built the way the critique assumes.
"Below ±25% materiality bar":** correct.
"No sensitivity analysis on baseline year":** UNVERIFIABLE. It comes from the thread, not from external evidence.
revised_hypothesis:
Stands as written. Add that the latest figure is 8.3M for 2024. Flag that the CG anchor year is an assumption. Strength: low-to-moderate, upward, non-material alone (+9–11%).

---
core_claim: Notified cases are ~8.2–8.3M, not ~7.5M, so a 7.5M baseline understates the starting point by ~9–11%.
core_claim_reason: Two successive WHO reports give 8.2M (2023) and 8.3M (2024) against 7.5M (2022).

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: A 2%/yr decline in notified case counts probably contradicts the observed trend; incidence rates fall slowly while counts do not
original.hypothesis: WHO's headline declines are in incidence *rates* per 100,000 (about 1–2%/yr in good pre-COVID years). Absolute case counts depend on population growth, which is large in the highest-burden countries (India, Nigeria, DRC, Pakistan, Philippines, Indonesia). Notified cases also reflect closing detection gaps (roughly 25% of incident cases are not notified), and WHO and national programmes are pushing active case-finding. If rate declines are roughly offset by population growth, absolute incident cases are roughly flat. If detection keeps improving, notifications could rise. CG applies a 2% annual decline to the count of cases. That is plausibly a different quantity from the one WHO reports as declining.
original.mechanism:
Scenario using my own arithmetic:
- Baseline 8.2M, flat for 8 years, × 0.96 × 0.90 → ~7.1M, about +29% versus 5.5M.
- A mild rise (+1%/yr) would give ~7.7M.
- A downside shock, such as the 2025 funding disruptions to TB programmes, could cut notifications. I cannot ground the size of that effect.

The 2%/yr figure therefore looks conservative for counts, and the error is probably in the upward direction (eligible ≈ 6.5–7.7M). Combined with Critique 1, this likely crosses the >25% threshold, but in the direction that improves cost-effectiveness.
suggested_evidence: WHO Global TB Report trends, which I recall showing global incident cases of ~10–11M and roughly flat in absolute terms since ~2015, with the rate falling ~8% over 2015–2023. I cannot cite exact values. Population growth is a logical argument. UNGROUNDED on specific numbers; needs verification.

evidence_found: Modelling of US funding cuts projects a 12–41% increase in TB episodes among people living with HIV in South Africa over 2025–2035.
If cuts persist, true incidence could rise, which pushes the same way as the critique.
The notification-versus-incidence distinction matters. A drug given at treatment start is exposed to notified/treated counts, which track detection, not the incidence-rate trend.
The critique's "direction: uncertain" label conflicts with its own conclusion ("probably upward"). Net direction is upward, with downside risk from funding.
Critique 2's scenario starts from the 8.2M baseline, so it already includes Critique 1. The two should not be added together.
caveats: WHO headline declines are in incidence rates:** VERIFIED.
The rate fell 1.7% between 2023 and 2024, and the net reduction from 2015 to 2024 was 12.3%.
Rate fell ~8% over 2015–2023:** VERIFIED.
The net reduction in the incidence rate between 2015 and 2023 was 8.3%.
Absolute incident cases roughly flat, ~10–11M:** VERIFIED for 2020–2024.
The total was 10.8M in 2023, up from 10.7M in 2022, 10.4M in 2021 and 10.1M in 2020.
The 2024 figure of 10.7M was a ~1% reduction from 2023.
I did not verify the "flat since ~2015" claim directly.
Population growth offsets rate declines:** VERIFIED.
Most of the increase in incident cases between 2022 and 2023 reflects population growth.

"~1–2%/yr in good pre-COVID years":** PARTLY WRONG, understated. The 2024 report slide says the 2015–2020 reduction was 12% , about 2.5%/yr. This weakens the "2% is clearly too fast" framing only for rates, not for counts.
~25% of incident cases not notified:** approximately right but slightly stale. The 2024 figure is 22% (78% notified). The gap was
2.7M in 2023, down from about 4M in 2020–21 and below the pre-pandemic 3.2M .
Notifications can rise as the detection gap closes:** VERIFIED. Notifications went from 7.1M (2019) to 8.3M (2024) while incident cases were flat.
Scenario arithmetic:** correct. 8.2 × 0.96 × 0.90 ≈ 7.1M (+29% vs 5.5M), and +1%/yr gives ≈ 7.7M.
2025 funding disruption could cut notifications:** PLAUSIBLE and now partly grounded.
WHO's provisional data for the first half of 2025 show a mixed picture, with reductions beyond trend in Cambodia, Kenya, Mozambique and Uganda.
WHO says impacts could worsen over time.
Modelling studies project excess TB deaths from USAID termination (420,500 by 2035) . The effect on global notified counts is not established. The critique's "cannot ground the size" is fair.
revised_hypothesis:
- Replace "roughly flat since ~2015" with "roughly flat 2020–2024".
- Correct pre-COVID rate declines to ~2.5%/yr, and the gap to ~22%.
- The conclusion is upward, not "uncertain": eligible ≈ 6.5–7.7M under flat-to-mild-growth scenarios, with a flagged downside from funding cuts.
- Flag that CG's use of 2% on counts is unverified.
- Strength: moderate-to-high, **upward**. It is likely material (>25%) when combined with the baseline correction, which is already inside its own scenario.

---
core_claim: Notified case counts have not been declining ~2%/yr and are more likely flat or rising over the next 8 years, so applying 2%/yr to counts understates eligible volume.
core_claim_reason: WHO data show incident counts flat and notifications up while rates fell only 1.7% in 2024.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: "Adult DS notified" is not "eligible for the trial label": missing applicability filters
original.hypothesis:
The 5.5M appears to be adults with drug-susceptible TB, but a statin adjunct would likely be indicated only for a subset.
- **Extrapulmonary TB** is ~15% of notified cases. If the proposed mechanism and outcomes (culture conversion, relapse, lung pathology) are pulmonary, these patients are outside the evidence.
- **Clinically diagnosed (not bacteriologically confirmed) cases** are ~35–40% of notifications globally. These patients lack culture endpoints, and some may not have TB.
- **Exclusions typical of a statin trial:** HIV coinfection (~6–8% of cases; ART interactions), pregnancy, hepatic disease, existing statin use, and drug-interaction contraindications.
- **Isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible TB** (Hr-TB, ~7% of cases) is classified as "DS" in some schemas but is treated with a different regimen. The 96% share may overstate trial-regimen-eligible patients.
original.mechanism:
Illustrative stack from my own multiplication:
- Pulmonary only: ×0.85 → ~4.7M.
- Add other filters (HIV, pregnancy, hepatic, Hr-TB), ×~0.85 → ~4.0M.
- Restrict to bacteriologically confirmed cases (×~0.62): ~2.5M.

Stacked with an overly conservative decline (Critique 2), this could net out to roughly the current figure. The filters should be modelled explicitly rather than implicitly. Applied alone and fully, they could push eligible below the 3.6M bar.
suggested_evidence: WHO Global TB Report for extrapulmonary share (~15–16%), bacteriological confirmation (~60–65%), and TB-HIV share. These are my recollections and should be verified. The statin exclusion list is my own inference from standard trial design and statin labelling, not from any specific protocol. Which filters apply depends on the trial design, which I have not seen.

evidence_found: WHO data confirm that the extrapulmonary share and the confirmation share vary a lot by region, so a global average could misstate a model weighted toward India, Nigeria and Indonesia.

The bacteriological-confirmation filter is design-dependent and probably the weakest link. A label or real-world adoption model would apply to all treated pulmonary DS-TB, not only culture-confirmed cases. WHO notes that a proportion of clinically diagnosed cases may be incorrect diagnoses of TB , which supports some downward adjustment but not a full ×0.62.
The critique's "could push eligible below the 3.6M bar" only occurs with the full confirmation filter. Without it, ~4.0M stays above the bar.
The filters partly overlap. HIV-positive and extrapulmonary cases are correlated, so multiplying them overstates the combined loss.
caveats: Extrapulmonary ≈ 15%:** VERIFIED, slightly low.
In 2024, 8.3 million were notified: 84% pulmonary and 16% extrapulmonary.
Regional variation is large.
Extrapulmonary share is 25% in South-East Asia and 8% in the Western Pacific.
It exceeds 20% in India, Bangladesh and Ethiopia.
India is the largest contributor, so the real filter loss is likely larger than 15%.
Clinically diagnosed ~35–40% of notifications:** MOSTLY CORRECT, but mislabelled.
64% of the 6.9M pulmonary cases were bacteriologically confirmed in 2024, up from 62% in 2023.

That is a share of pulmonary cases, so it is ~36% clinically diagnosed among pulmonary cases. The critique's own stack applies ×0.62 after the pulmonary filter, which is correct sequencing. Confirmed pulmonary cases are ~54% of all notifications (0.84 × 0.64).
HIV coinfection ~6–8%:** ROUGHLY CORRECT.
413,516 notified TB cases were in people with HIV in 2024, equal to 6.2% of the 6.7M with an HIV test result.
That is about 5% of all notifications.
In 2023 the figure was 6.8%.
The range is fine for tested cases but slightly high for all notifications.
Hr-TB ~7%:** VERIFIED.
Data reported to WHO from 156 countries (2002–2018) gave 7.4% of new patients and 11.4% of previously treated patients.
Other sources say about 8% (range 5–11%) . The treatment difference is verified.
WHO recommended a distinct 6-month regimen for Hr-TB containing rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and levofloxacin.
The claim that Hr-TB is classified as "DS" in some schemas is UNVERIFIABLE. It depends on CG's schema, and Hr-TB patients are usually not detected without isoniazid testing.
Stack arithmetic:** correct. 5.5 × 0.85 = 4.7M; × 0.85 = 4.0M; × 0.62 = 2.5M.

Statin exclusion list (pregnancy, hepatic disease, ART interaction, existing statin use):** UNVERIFIABLE as a trial design. This is the investigator's inference, which the investigator discloses. It is plausible. Rifampicin–statin interactions are real, and I did not check them against a protocol.
Pregnancy filter:** The size is not grounded in any search result.
revised_hypothesis:
- Keep the verified shares: extrapulmonary 16% (up to 25% in SE Asia), pulmonary bacteriological confirmation 64%, HIV ~5–6%, Hr-TB ~7–8%.
- Flag the statin-specific exclusions and the pregnancy and hepatic filters as **UNGROUNDED — plausible but needs a trial protocol**.
- Treat the bacteriological-confirmation filter as scenario-dependent rather than a base-case reduction.
- Account for filter overlap.
- Realistic range: ~3.5–4.7M before any confirmation restriction; ~2.5M only under a culture-confirmed-only design.
- Direction: **downward** if filters are not already in the model. The "uncertain" label arises only from Critique 2 offsetting it.
- Strength: moderate. It is conditional on CG's model structure and on trial design.
core_claim: CG's 5.5M includes cases outside the likely trial or label population (extrapulmonary, HIV, pregnancy, hepatic disease, Hr-TB, clinically diagnosed), and these should be modelled explicitly.
core_claim_reason: The WHO shares are verified, but whether CG's 5.5M already excludes them, and which filters a trial or label would apply, are not visible or verifiable.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: Shorter and new regimens erode both the eligible population and the incremental benefit
original.hypothesis:
By ~2033, a meaningful share of DS-TB patients may be on regimens other than the 6-month HRZE the trial tests.
- WHO (2022) recommended a 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen (HPMZ, from Study 31/A5349, Dorman et al., NEJM 2021) for people aged 12 and over.
- Other pipeline options include TRUNCATE-TB-type strategies (Paton et al., NEJM 2023, from my recollection) and bedaquiline-containing short regimens.

Consequences:
1. **Applicability:** a statin trial on HRZE does not establish efficacy on a rifapentine- or moxifloxacin-based backbone. Rifapentine is a stronger CYP3A4 inducer than rifampicin, so the interaction problem may worsen. Re-trialing on new backbones would add cost and time that the model may not count.
2. **Incremental value:** shorter, more potent regimens may lower baseline relapse and mortality. This leaves less room for an adjunct to add benefit, if the benefit is defined relative to standard-regimen outcomes.
3. **Mechanism:** if the statin's value is in shortening treatment, a 4-month regimen leaves less to shorten.
original.mechanism: If 20–40% of eligible patients are on non-trial regimens at the benefit horizon, effective eligible falls ~20–40%, from 5.5M to ~3.3–4.4M. That is at or near the 3.6M bar. If the effect size also shrinks on newer backbones, the effect compounds. The 20–40% adoption range is my own scenario and is not grounded in published projections. Programme uptake of HPMZ has so far been slow because of rifapentine supply and cost, so the low end is more likely than the high end.
suggested_evidence: Dorman et al. (NEJM 2021) and WHO 2022 guidance exist. The adoption forecast is UNGROUNDED, so this is an inference. The interaction claim for rifapentine and atorvastatin is pharmacological reasoning, not a cited study.

evidence_found: HPMZ is restricted to age ≥12, and it is conditional. Rifapentine exposure has been shown to drive outcomes: low rifapentine exposure is the strongest driver of TB-related unfavorable outcomes in the rifapentine-moxifloxacin arm.
That limits how fast HPMZ can displace HRZE, because dosing and supply constraints apply. It weakly favours the low end of the Investigator's range.
Under the WHO guidance, adolescents aged 12–16 have three options: 4-month HPMZ, 4-month 2HRZ(E)/2HR, or standard 6-month 2HRZ(E)/4HR.

The 4-month HRZ(E) regimen for children with non-severe TB still contains rifampicin. The rifamycin-induction problem would therefore remain on that backbone, which weakens the "non-trial backbone" argument for that group.
Most 2022 TRUNCATE-type and bedaquiline-linezolid strategies remain trial-stage. They are unlikely to reach 20–40% of patients by 2033.
caveats: WHO recommended the 4-month HPMZ regimen in 2022 for age ≥12: **VERIFIED** (see above).
A statin trial on HRZE does not establish efficacy on a rifapentine/moxifloxacin backbone: **PLAUSIBLE.** This is sound reasoning, and I found no direct evidence either way.

"Rifapentine is a stronger CYP3A4 inducer than rifampicin": **UNVERIFIABLE and probably overstated.** I ran out of searches before checking it. From general pharmacology, rifampicin is usually described as the most potent inducer, and rifapentine is comparable or somewhat weaker depending on dose. Both are inducers, so the broader worry about interactions with atorvastatin survives. The comparative "stronger" claim should be dropped or checked.

"Programme uptake of HPMZ has been slow because of rifapentine supply and cost": **UNVERIFIABLE.** I found no direct source. One adjacent source says use of the regimen in clinical practice may be limited by the high rifapentine dose, particularly in patients with comorbidities.
This partly supports the idea that uptake is constrained, though for a different reason than the Investigator gives.
20–40% of eligible patients on non-trial regimens by ~2033: **UNGROUNDED.** The Investigator says so too. I found no projection.
Shorter regimens reduce room for an adjunct to add benefit: **PLAUSIBLE.** This is logic only.
revised_hypothesis:
The 6-month HRZE regimen is no longer the only standard of care. 
WHO conditionally recommends a 4-month HPMZ regimen for people aged 12 or older
, and Paton et al. (NEJM 2023) showed that an 8-week bedaquiline-linezolid strategy was noninferior to standard treatment in a trial. Three things follow:
- Efficacy shown on an HRZE backbone may not transfer to rifapentine/moxifloxacin regimens. Rifapentine is a CYP3A4 inducer, so the atorvastatin interaction question carries over. Whether it is stronger than rifampicin is unverified.
- Shorter regimens may leave less baseline relapse or mortality for an adjunct to improve.
- Any statin benefit that works through shortening treatment would be reduced.

The share of patients moved off HRZE by ~2033 is **UNGROUNDED, plausible but needs empirical support**. Evidence of dosing and supply limits suggests the share may be modest. Direction: uncertain, magnitude: low-to-medium (down from medium), because the displacement estimate has no support and the evidence points to slow uptake.

---
core_claim: 20–40% of eligible patients will be on non-HRZE regimens at the benefit horizon, which pushes effective eligibility down to about the 3.6M threshold.
core_claim_reason: No adoption projection exists, and the Investigator admits it is a self-chosen scenario. The slow-uptake evidence points to the low end of the range or below it.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: M72/AS01E and other incidence shocks are likely not large enough by year 8–10, but should be modelled
original.hypothesis:
The Phase III of M72/AS01E (started 2024, ~20,000 participants, results expected late 2020s from my recollection of Gates MRI materials) follows a Phase IIb (Tait et al., NEJM 2019) that reported ~50% efficacy against progression to pulmonary TB in already-infected adults. If Phase III succeeds, licensure could come ~2028–30, with rollout starting thereafter.

The 30–50% incidence reduction that would be material is unlikely by 2033–35:
- Rollout is slow. Adolescent and adult programmes need Gavi financing and new delivery platforms.
- Vaccine impact accrues gradually, mostly by preventing progression in already-infected people.

My own estimate is a 5–15% reduction in incidence by 2033–35, which on its own would not cross the threshold. LSHTM-type models (e.g. Harris et al.) project larger impacts mostly in the 2040s. I cannot cite a specific figure from them.

The vaccine effect matters more over the *benefit horizon*. If atorvastatin benefit accrues across many years after adoption, a vaccine could reduce the eligible pool by 30–50% in the later years. CG's constant 5.5M "eligible at 8y" ignores the downward trajectory after that point.
original.mechanism: Effect on eligible at year 8: –5 to –15%, i.e. ~4.7–5.2M. If the benefit horizon extends beyond ~15 years, average eligible over that horizon could be ~20–35% lower, depending on how the horizon is modelled. I cannot determine this without seeing how the CEA treats post-adoption years (**magnitude uncertain, requires CEA sensitivity analysis**). The probability of vaccine success should be weighted separately (the Phase IIb efficacy estimate was in a small, selected population).
suggested_evidence: Tait et al. (NEJM 2019) for the Phase IIb. The Phase III timeline is from my recollection of Gates MRI. The modelling is a general recollection that I cannot cite precisely. UNGROUNDED on the specific impact numbers.

evidence_found: Models assume ~10-year duration of protection, 50% efficacy and staggered introduction. For example, the India model assumed introduction in 2025 with repeat campaigns in 2035 and 2045.

Vaccine timing therefore matters a great deal. With later introduction, around 2030, impact by 2033–35 is likely small. This supports the Investigator's claim of a small effect at year 8 and a larger one later.
A baseline assumption matters here. The India model assumed scale-up of non-vaccine interventions to meet a 50% reduction in incidence by 2035 versus 2015.
The CEA's eligible-population baseline should be checked for the same kind of decline.
A South Africa model found M72 could avert between 0.86 and 2.55 million TB cases by 2050 . That is large cumulatively but consistent with back-loaded impact.
A demand-forecast paper exists (
"Preparing for Tuberculosis Vaccine M72/AS01E Implementation"
). It could inform uptake assumptions but I did not extract numbers from it.
caveats: Phase IIb efficacy applied to an already-infected population: **VERIFIED.**
The trial enrolled 3,573 HIV-negative adults aged 18–50 in Southern Africa with evidence of M.tb infection (IGRA+).
Phase IIb evidence is "small, selected": **VERIFIED.**
Only 39 participants contributed to the primary efficacy analysis: 13 vaccinated and 26 placebo.
The confidence interval is very wide.

Results are expected in the late 2020s and licensure around 2028–30: **PLAUSIBLE, not directly confirmed.** The event-driven design implies several years of accrual after a ~2-year enrolment period. I found no official timeline.
Incidence reduction of 5–15% by 2033–35: **UNVERIFIABLE.** This is the Investigator's own estimate.

Vaccine impact accrues gradually, mostly via already-infected people: **PARTIALLY CONTRADICTED / nuanced.** Harris et al. conclude M72 would be effective in a larger proportion of the population than BCG-revaccination and have a more rapid impact on tuberculosis incidence.

Post-infection vaccines act on the prevalent latent pool, so they are faster than infection-blocking vaccines. They are still limited by coverage ramp-up and duration of protection. Separately, a vaccine with pre- and post-infection efficacy had a much greater 2050 incidence impact than a post-infection-only vaccine.
That supports a modest impact from a post-infection-only M72.
Average eligible pool 20–35% lower over a >15-year horizon: **UNVERIFIABLE.** The Investigator says so. It depends on assumptions about vaccine uptake, duration and coverage.
revised_hypothesis: Tait et al. (NEJM 2019) reported a vaccine efficacy of 49.7% (95% CI 2.1–74.2) against pulmonary TB in about 3,500 HIV-negative, IGRA-positive adults. The primary analysis rested on only 39 cases, so the point estimate is imprecise. The Phase III, which started in March 2024, is ongoing with a target of about 26,000 participants. Licensure and rollout timing are uncertain but unlikely to produce a large incidence effect by 2033–35. Published models (Harris et al. and related work) project cumulative impact toward 2050 and a smaller effect from post-infection-only vaccines. The CEA should therefore be checked for whether it holds the eligible pool constant after year 8. Any later-year reduction in eligibility (30–50%) and the 20–35% averaged reduction are **UNGROUNDED, plausible but needing empirical support** via CEA sensitivity analysis. Vaccine success probability should be weighted separately. Direction: decreases, magnitude: low-to-medium and horizon-dependent, with the "5–15% at year 8" figure marked as the Investigator's own estimate.
core_claim: M72-driven incidence reduction by year 8–10 is small (5–15%). It becomes large (30–50%) only later, so a constant eligible-population assumption overstates the pool in the later years of the benefit horizon.
core_claim_reason: The model literature points to impact building toward 2050 and a modest effect from a post-infection-only vaccine, but no source gives 2033–35 incidence figures, and the 30–50% later-year reduction is not sourced.
